title: Futures vs Stocks
hook: A futures chart might look like every other chart. What you're trading underneath it isn't the same.

launchpad.outcome: Name the structural differences between trading futures and trading stocks, not just "futures move faster."
launchpad.missionQuestion: Can you treat 10 shares of a stock and 10 futures contracts as the same size?

markers.label: Stocks vs. futures side by side
Know what one unit is worth

slides.headline: A share isn’t a contract.
slides.line: Different thing. Different unit. Different risk.

cards.label: Stock
cards.sub: A claim on owning a piece of a company.

cards.label: Futures contract
cards.sub: An agreement based on price movement. No ownership.

check.prompt: What’s the core difference between them?

options.label: Same thing, different names
options.feedback: They’re structurally different. One is ownership, one isn’t.

options.label: Ownership vs. agreement
options.why: Buying a stock means owning a piece of a company. A futures contract carries no ownership stake at all.

slides.headline: Expiration. Rollover. Margin.
slides.line: Futures have a contract month, may roll into the next contract, and use different margin. No need to master it today.

check.prompt: She wants to profit from a short-term move and doesn’t care about owning the company. Which is built for that?

options.label: Stocks
options.feedback: Stock ownership is fundamentally about owning a piece of a company, not short-term price speculation.

options.label: Futures
options.why: Futures contracts are built purely around price movement, with no ownership stake.

options.label: Nothing, 10 is 10
options.feedback: The unit matters. 10 shares of a stock and 10 futures contracts are not comparable sizes.

options.label: The unit is different
options.why: Right. Share quantity and contract quantity aren’t equivalent units of risk. 10 shares and 10 contracts can carry wildly different dollar risk.

slides.quote: Position size only means something when you understand what one unit of your instrument is worth.

slides.prompt: Why can’t you just trade as many contracts as you used to trade shares?
slides.modelAnswer: Because a share and a contract aren't the same unit of risk. One share of a stock might be worth $50, while one futures contract's point value could be worth $2, $5, or $50 per point depending on the instrument. The number 10 doesn't mean anything on its own.

takeaways: Stocks are ownership; futures are standardized contracts on price movement.
Futures contracts expire and involve rollover, stocks don't.
Share count and contract count are not equivalent units of risk.
remember: Know what one unit of your instrument is actually worth.
